Now that AI is part of everyday marketing work, teams need a different kind of shared folder. Within a year, I expect every marketing team that builds seriously with AI to have one. For many, it will be GitHub.

Google Drive and SharePoint were built for people reading documents. An AI setup is a system of small files that depend on each other. The positioning file feeds the voice guide. The voice guide feeds every writing skill. Change one, and the output of ten others changes with it.

Without the right home for those files, the same thing happens in team after team. Five people build five versions of the same voice guide. Someone improves a skill, and nobody else knows. Every switch to a new AI vendor creates a mess.

Here’s what an AI system needs as an underlying infrastructure and what document tools handle poorly:

- A history of every change, and why it was made – when the AI starts sounding off-brand, you can find what changed.

- A safe way back – one step returns everything to how it was yesterday.

- Independence from any one AI vendor – plain files any AI tool can read, owned by your company.

## Maya solved this without any technical skills or support

Maya Pasek, Head of Content at Bluestone PIM, ran into exactly the same problem with her team. She solved it with GitHub, without any technical skills or support.

Today her team keeps all of its AI knowledge and automations in one shared place, and everyone’s AI tool reads from it. When someone builds a new skill, the whole team has it straight away. And when a better model comes along, they can switch without losing anything.

Before I tell you how she did it, a short detour on what GitHub actually is. If you already know, skip ahead.

## GitHub in plain English

GitHub is a shared online folder with memory. Developers use it to work on the same code without overwriting each other. It works just as well for plain text documents.

A folder on GitHub is called a repository, or repo. Two things make it useful for marketers:

- It remembers every change. Each update is saved with a short note on who changed what and why. You can go back to any earlier version.

- Everyone works from the same copy. When someone saves changes to the shared repo (this is called pushing), everyone else gets them.

A marketing team’s repo holds two kinds of files most often:

- Knowledge files: what the company does, who it’s for, the brand voice, the objections prospects raise.

- Skills: saved instructions that teach the AI how to do a recurring task your team’s way.

Each person connects their AI tool to the repo. From then on, everyone’s AI knows the same things and has the same skills. One person’s improvement becomes the whole team’s. And the knowledge stays with your company, whatever AI tool you use next.

Keep the repo private. If your developers already use GitHub, ask IT for a repo inside the company account. GitLab and Bitbucket work the same way, if that’s what your company uses.

## How Maya did it

### It started with a pile of files on one laptop

Maya was the first person on her team to get obsessed with AI tools. Her word, not mine.

By the time the company bought AI subscriptions for everyone, she had built a pile of skills and documents. All of it sat on her laptop, so only she could use it. She wanted her colleagues to run them in their own Claude, and GitHub turned out to be the way to share them.

### Why not just use a Claude Project?

She gets this question a lot and her answer is the part of this story I keep coming back to.

Her team has switched AI tools twice, from ChatGPT to Gemini and then to Claude. Both moves were messy, and some projects were stranded in the old tools.

Claude is popular right now, but Maya doesn’t want the team to depend on it. With the files in GitHub, the next move means pointing a new tool at the same folder.

### The content brain

The first thing Maya put in the repo is what she calls the content brain , a set of files that explain:

- what the company does

- its positioning

- its unique selling points

- its target audience

- its brand voice

- the questions and concerns of prospects, pulled from sales call transcripts

These files sync automatically to everyone’s Claude. Anyone who builds a new skill starts from them instead of from zero.

It’s the same idea as the “source of truth” files in Ryan Law’s first-day plan, which I translated a while ago in my article Content marketing is getting technical. That’s not the problem . Ahrefs has developers. Maya’s team is a regular marketing team. They arrived at the same foundation.

That foundation is what matters. AI multiplies what you already do, including what you do badly. A skill built on vague positioning produces vague content, faster. The content brain is where the strategy lives, so every automation inherits it.

### Skills on top, shared instantly

On top of the content brain, the team builds skills. One of them sends Maya a monthly report with all the numbers they need, plus suggestions on what to double down on.

The bigger change, she says, is the sharing. Someone builds a skill in Claude Code (the version of Claude that works directly with files and folders), pushes it to GitHub, and everyone has it straight away.

The team now works exclusively in Claude Code. Maya estimates it saves about 20 hours a week. Skills handle much of the research, reporting and content creation, and there are fewer meetings. People on the team mostly direct the work and edit.

### Was it easy? Not really.

That was Maya’s answer, with a laugh.

Getting everyone connected to the same repo took a while. She ran a three-hour workshop on connecting to GitHub, what Claude Code can do and how to build automations.

The hardest part is for the people to get used to it. In her view, the words “code” and “repo” scare people off more than the actual work does.

When she gets stuck, she sends Claude Code a few screenshots and asks what to do next. The tool that seems intimidating is also the one teaching her how to use it.

## So, will marketers use GitHub every day within a year?

Louise de Sadeleer recently wrote that marketers will need a GitHub repo to be hireable within a year. I said she was directionally right, but that it won’t be the bar for everyone.

What I do believe is that marketers will open GitHub as part of their daily routine within a year. At least on teams building seriously with AI.

Once a team has more than a handful of shared skills and source files, it needs a home for them that is shared, versioned and vendor-neutral. Developers solved that problem years ago.

For many teams, not yet. Someone has to do what Maya did: build the first files, set up the repo, run the workshop. In a lot of teams, that person hasn’t stepped up yet.

## The career opportunity

Maya made one more point I want to underline. Learning this and sharing it with colleagues builds a strong internal reputation. Most people don’t have the time, or the curiosity, to learn these tools. That leaves a big opening for those who do.

She didn’t wait for a mandate or a budget. She built something useful, noticed it was stuck on her laptop, and made it everyone’s. That’s the marketer AI can’t replace: someone who has built something other people use and get results from.

## Try it this week

Maya’s advice is simple: just start.

- Create a GitHub account and a private repository.

- Connect Claude Code to it. If you get stuck, send a screenshot and ask what’s next.

- Save one file there. Start with your positioning: what you do, who it’s for and why it’s different. Every future skill will need it.
